title: The Power of Connection: Elevate Your Leadership with Simple Acts of Care
author: Heather McGonigal
summary: Coach Heather McGonigal argues that busy people drift into moving through other people the way they move through tasks, trading information and then moving on. Her remedy is simple attention: noticing when a colleague is quieter than usual, when someone says they are fine but sounds otherwise, or when a neighbour needs a little more presence and a little less efficiency. She proposes a two-minute practice, staying briefly after a meeting to ask another question, listen without looking at a phone and let the person know they matter. She is careful to say that caring does not mean abandoning boundaries or taking responsibility for everyone else's needs, since there is a wide space between responsibility for someone and presence with them. The piece ends with an invitation to linger one moment longer than usual this week, and it is part three of her Coach Heather Fundamentals series on being a good human.
points: Leaders can slip into treating people as part of the task flow, and the antidote is deliberately noticing the person in front of them.
A two-minute check-in after a meeting is offered as a small, concrete act that builds a bridge between colleagues.
Care means listening without a phone and asking the extra question, not fixing the other person's problem or finding perfect words.
Healthy boundaries remain intact, because presence is different from taking responsibility for everyone else's needs.
Offering attention is restorative for the giver as well as the receiver, which makes connection a sustainable leadership habit.
quotes: And sometimes, without meaning to, we can start moving through people that way too.
I believe one of the simplest ways we can be good humans to one another is to slow down enough to actually see the person in front of us.
Two minutes more after a meeting to check in with a coworker can build a bridge that says we are humans in this together.
Care doesn’t always require a grand gesture. Sometimes it looks like staying two minutes longer.
Of course, we cannot give unlimited time and energy to every person we encounter. Caring for others does not mean abandoning our own boundaries or taking responsibility for everyone else’s needs.
There is something deeply restorative about being genuinely seen by another human being. And there is something restorative about offering that kind of presence, too.
Sometimes being a good human is simply deciding not to rush past another human being.
